 ALBANY, N.Y. (WKTV) -- A child in Lewis County has died from measles, marking the first measles-related death in New York State in more than 30 years.
 The New York State Department of Health and Lewis County Public Health shared the news in a joint statement, noting the child’s death is linked to an ongoing measles outbreak.
 Officials extended condolences to the family and urged respect for their privacy.
 The agencies stressed that measles is highly contagious and can cause serious complications and death.
 They encouraged everyone to make sure they are up to date on measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations and to speak with healthcare providers about immunizations.
 Governor Kathy Hochul, in a statement, called the death “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
 Hochul said, “In New York, we will continue to stand by proven public health measures and do everything we can to keep New Yorkers safe and healthy.”
 The Department of Health said it has provided resources to Lewis County to help with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts.
 The department is also working with county health departments and local partners to offer the MMR vaccine to anyone unvaccinated who requests it and to closely monitor and investigate all reported cases.
 Officials reported that as of Oct. 24, there have been 178 measles cases this year, with 170 in New York State outside of the city and eight in New York City.
 The Department of Health recommended that infants six months and older receive an early dose of the MMR vaccine if they are traveling or living in a community with measles transmission.
 One dose of the vaccine provides 93% protection, while two doses provide 97% protection.
 Measles symptoms can include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, usually appearing seven to 14 days after infection. A rash often develops three to five days after symptoms start.
 Officials urged anyone unsure of their vaccination status to contact a healthcare provider or local health department.
 They also advised people who are sick to call ahead before visiting a clinic or emergency department so infection-control steps can be taken.
